tldr: In frictional contact dynamics, this work preserves the hard-contact forward solve while relaxing the entire Coulomb friction cone along a central path only in the backward pass to compute smooth analytic gradients. This enables policy learning on a desktop PC that transfers directly to a real quadruped robot using just a single environment, 100,000 samples, and less than 2 minutes of training.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed differentiable contact framework. The forward pass solves exact hard contact to preserve physical feasibility, while the backward pass relaxes the de Saxcé-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem along a central path to analytically compute contact sensitivities.
overview:
In legged locomotion control, contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) and policy gradient learning via differentiable simulation (BPTT) are drawing significant attention as powerful paradigms. However, differentiating physics simulations exactly yields gradients restricted solely to the current contact mode (the discrete "separating, clamping, or sliding" states). When a foot is clamped to the ground, first-order gradient information toward "liftoff" or "sliding" becomes zero, leaving the optimization stuck in its initial contact state.

To solve this, the authors propose an asymmetric design: keep the forward solve as exact hard contact, and smoothly relax the contact conditions along a central path only during backward gradient computation. The frictional contact problem is unified into a single second-order-cone complementarity problem (SOCCP) via the de Saxcé correction, and analytically differentiated using Jordan algebra while preserving the coupled normal-tangential sensitivities. A Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution finds the relaxed evaluation point quickly and accurately.

Using this gradient, trajectory optimization for a quadruped robot autonomously generates foot-stepping adjustments and sliding-braking motions in response to obstacles and external forces. In policy learning, training in a single environment (1 env) without parallel workers produced trotting, pacing, and ungait-conditioned locomotion policies on a desktop PC in just 100,000 samples and 108 seconds, which transferred directly to a physical quadruped robot. Real-world experiments demonstrated high robustness, including traversing debris, resisting pushes, and recovering from slips on low-friction surfaces.
contributions: Formulating a framework that keeps the hard-contact solve intact in the forward pass while relaxing the entire Coulomb friction condition along a central path in the backward pass to analytically compute coupled sensitivities
Deriving an analytic contact gradient that remains continuous across separating, clamping, and sliding modes, and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation parameter vanishes
Achieving zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of quadruped locomotion policies using single-environment BPTT with just 100,000 samples and under 2 minutes of training
Demonstrating autonomous foot stepping and sliding-braking behaviors in contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO) that were impossible with exact or normal-only relaxed gradients

sections.heading: Breaking through the barrier of contact differentiation
sections.summary: Differentiable simulation is a powerful tool for contact-rich robot control, but exact contact sensitivity is confined within the current contact mode and provides no direction toward mode transitions. This paper proposes a gradient method that preserves the physical feasibility of the forward pass while relaxing friction-cone complementarity along a central path only in the backward pass to smoothly connect contact modes.
sections.details:
There are two primary paradigms for controlling robots that move by interacting with the ground. One is policy learning, such as reinforcement learning, and the other is contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO), which plans contact timing and locations simultaneously. Differentiating the simulator itself to extract first-order gradients (Jacobians) has gained traction, but applying it to legged locomotion has faced a major barrier.

When calculating the exact sensitivity of contact dynamics, the resulting gradient is restricted to the current active set (contact mode). For instance, when a foot is clamped to the ground, linearization only sees directions where clamping is maintained, and first-order information toward lifting off or slipping is completely zero. As a result, optimization algorithms cannot break out of their initial contact mode.

Prior works either modified the forward pass into soft contact, which sacrifices physical fidelity, or relaxed only the normal direction (Signorini condition), which loses coupled tangential friction and slip information. In this work, the authors formulate Coulomb frictional contact as a single second-order-cone complementarity problem via the de Saxcé correction, and propose an analytic gradient that smoothly relaxes both normal and tangential directions along its central path only in the backward pass. This maintains hard-contact feasibility during forward rollouts while providing informative gradient pathways across separating, clamping, and sliding modes during backpropagation.

sections.heading: The evolution of differentiable contact and trajectory optimization
sections.summary: This section reviews contact simulation formulations, sensitivity methods, policy learning with differentiable simulation, and conventional CITO approaches. It highlights the novelty of leaving the forward pass unchanged while independently relaxing the full friction cone during backpropagation.
sections.details:
Prior work is categorized from three perspectives:

### II-A Contact Simulation and Differentiable Contact
Rigid-body frictional contact is defined by three coupled conditions: the Signorini condition (normal non-penetration), the Coulomb friction cone, and the principle of maximum dissipation (MDP). Methods for computing derivatives include finite differences (computational cost scales with input dimension), automatic differentiation (high memory consumption and numerical instability), and analytic methods via implicit differentiation at the solution. This work belongs to the analytic category, but it critically departs from prior work by shifting from the hard-contact solution to a relaxed point on the central path for evaluation.

### II-B Differentiable Simulation for Policy Learning
Model-free RL, such as PPO, dominates legged locomotion, but reward-based zeroth-order estimators (REINFORCE) suffer from high variance and require massive sample budgets. First-order learning via backpropagation through time (BPTT) is sample-efficient, but contact discontinuities cause exploding or vanishing gradients. Previous approaches softened contact detection with sigmoids—distorting the forward rollout—or relied on simplified single-rigid-body surrogates. This work maintains exact multi-body hard contact in the forward pass while training hardware-viable policies via BPTT in a single environment.

### II-C Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization (CITO)
CITO formulations include direct transcription (e.g., orthogonal collocation with contact forces as decision variables) and shooting methods (DDP/iLQR) that leverage simulation transition Jacobians. To smooth contact sensitivities in shooting methods, prior works differentiated intermediate iterations of interior-point solvers or relaxed only the normal direction. However, the former ties the relaxation level to solver convergence, while the latter misses tangential slip information. This work resolves these issues by delivering a full friction-cone relaxation optimized specifically for the backward pass.

sections.heading: Fundamentals of contact mechanics and optimal control: Mathematical formulation
sections.summary: This section details how transition Jacobians are structured for shooting-based DDP and BPTT policy learning, alongside per-timestep contact impulse problems. It introduces the de Saxcé correction that unifies Coulomb friction into an SOCCP, and derives exact sensitivities under fixed contact modes.
sections.details:
The underlying mathematical framework is organized as follows:

### III-A Optimal Control Problem and Transition Jacobians
For discrete-time dynamics $\bm{x}_{t+1}=f(\bm{x}_{t},\bm{u}_{t})$, trajectory optimization (DDP/iLQR) optimizes open-loop control sequences $\bm{u}_{0:H-1}$, while BPTT policy learning optimizes feedback policy parameters $\theta$. Both rely on backward propagation through the transition Jacobians $f_x := \partial\bm{x}_{t+1}/\partial\bm{x}_{t}$ and $f_u := \partial\bm{x}_{t+1}/\partial\bm{u}_{t}$.

### III-B Multi-Body Contact Dynamics and Contact Modes
Under semi-implicit Euler velocity-level integration, next-step relative contact velocity $\bm{\sigma}$ and contact impulse $\bm{\lambda}$ are coupled through the Delassus relation $\bm{\sigma} = A\bm{\lambda} + \bm{b}$, where $A$ is the apparent inverse inertia matrix and $\bm{b}$ is the free-motion term. For single-point contact, states split into three modes:
- Separating: normal impulse $\lambda_N = 0$, relative normal velocity $\sigma_N \ge 0$
- Clamping: $\bm{\sigma} = \bm{0}$, tangential impulse inside the friction cone $\lVert\bm{\lambda}_T\rVert \le \mu\lambda_N$
- Sliding: $\sigma_N = 0$, tangential impulse on the friction cone boundary $\bm{\lambda}_T = -\mu\lambda_N (\bm{\sigma}_T / \lVert\bm{\sigma}_T\rVert)$

### III-C SOCCP Formulation via the de Saxcé Correction
The Signorini condition, Coulomb friction cone, and maximum dissipation principle are unified into a single conic complementarity condition by adding the de Saxcé correction term $\Gamma_\mu(\bm{\sigma}) = (\mu\lVert\bm{\sigma}_T\rVert, 0, 0)^\top$ to the normal velocity. Expressed via the Jordan product $\circ$ on self-dual second-order cones (SOC), this yields a compact second-order-cone complementarity problem (SOCCP): $\tilde{\bm{\lambda}} \circ \tilde{\bm{\sigma}} = \bm{0}$ for scaled variables $\tilde{\bm{\lambda}}$ and $\tilde{\bm{\sigma}}$.

### III-D Limitations of Exact Contact Sensitivity
Differentiating this condition with fixed contact modes yields $d\bm{\lambda}=\bm{0}$ in separating and $d\bm{\sigma}=\bm{0}$ in clamping. First-order gradient information toward neighboring contact modes is entirely lost.

sections.heading: Why is relaxing the entire friction cone necessary?
sections.summary: Using a point-mass model, this section demonstrates how exact mode-fixed sensitivities cause optimization to stall when contact transitions are required. Relaxing only the normal direction proves insufficient, showing that relaxing the full friction cone with coupled normal and tangential directions is indispensable.
sections.details:
In optimization, differentiating the loss through contact point motion can be expressed as $(\partial\ell/\partial\bm{\sigma})(d\bm{\sigma}/d\eta)$. In clamping mode, however, the mode constraint enforces $d\bm{\sigma}/d\eta = \bm{0}$. Even when moving the foot would decrease the loss, the gradient becomes zero, and optimization terminates prematurely.

To examine this, the paper evaluates three reaching tasks using a 1 kg planar point-mass model optimized from zero-input initialization:
1. Reaching upward (requires a transition from clamping to separating)
2. Reaching horizontally (requires lifting off from clamping, translating, and clamping again)
3. Pulling back an overshooting mass with initial velocity (requires landing from separating, and applying frictional braking to return to the target)

The exact gradient failed across all tasks because the mass remained clamped in place. The Signorini-relaxed gradient (normal-only relaxation) succeeded in Task 1 (upward reach), but failed in Tasks 2 and 3 due to the absence of tangential gradients. In contrast, only the proposed method—relaxing the full friction cone—found the optimal trajectories with appropriate jumping and sliding braking across all three tasks, matching global optima obtained via mixed-integer quadratic programming (MIQP). Coupled tangential-normal relaxation is essential for discovering contact-mode transitions.

sections.heading: Proposed method: Analytic contact sensitivity via relaxed de Saxcé conic complementarity
sections.summary: The complementarity condition is relaxed along a central path parameter $\rho > 0$, matrixified using the Jordan product, and analytically differentiated. A residual-regularized Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution solves for the evaluation point, accompanied by a normal velocity offset for numerical robustness.
sections.details:
Mathematical derivation and algorithm details of the proposed sensitivity calculation:

### V-A Central-Path Relaxation and Unified Contact Sensitivity
The complementarity condition is relaxed along the central path as $\tilde{\bm{\lambda}} \circ \tilde{\bm{\sigma}} = \rho \bm{e}$ with $\rho > 0$ and cone identity $\bm{e}=(1,0,0)^\top$, shifting variables from the boundary into the cone interior ($\mathrm{int}\,\mathcal{K}$). Differentiating this relation using the arrow matrix $L(\cdot)$ of the Jordan product yields:
$$\mathcal{M}_{\lambda}\, d\bm{\lambda} + \mathcal{M}_{\sigma}\, d\bm{\sigma} = \bm{0}$$
where $\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} = L(\tilde{\bm{\sigma}})C$ and $\mathcal{M}_{\sigma} = L(\tilde{\bm{\lambda}})D(\bm{\sigma})$. Combining this with the differentiated Delassus relation $d\bm{\sigma} = A\,d\bm{\lambda} + (dA)\bm{\lambda} + d\bm{b}$ yields a unified sensitivity equation across all contact modes:
$$(\mathcal{M}_{\lambda} + \mathcal{M}_{\sigma}A)\, d\bm{\lambda} = -\mathcal{M}_{\sigma}((dA)\bm{\lambda} + d\bm{b})$$

### V-B Computing the Evaluation Point via Newton Iteration
This derivative must be evaluated at the relaxed solution $(\bm{\lambda}^\star, \bm{\sigma}^\star)$ for $\rho > 0$. The proposed method initializes from the forward hard-contact solution $(\bm{\lambda}_h, \bm{\sigma}_h)$ and applies a Newton solver with residual-proportional diagonal regularization $\beta\lVert F_\rho\rVert I$ to converge within a few iterations. This avoids Jacobian near-singularities near the friction cone boundary.

### V-C Normal Free-Velocity Offset and Theoretical Consistency
To enhance numerical stability and encourage contact liftoff exploration, a positive offset $\delta$ is added to the normal Delassus term during the backward pass only ($\hat{b}_N = b_N + \delta$). The paper also proves theoretically that in the limit $\rho \to 0^+$ (with $\delta=0$), the proposed sensitivity matches the exact mode-fixed sensitivity across separating, clamping, and sliding modes.

captions.F5: Overall computational flow of the proposed method. The forward pass solves exact hard contact, while the backward pass relaxes the de Saxcé SOCCP along the central path ($\rho>0$), computes the evaluation point $(\bm{\lambda}^\star, \bm{\sigma}^\star)$ via Newton iteration, and analytically derives sensitivities for policy learning and DDP.

sections.heading: Implementation on a quadruped robot: BPTT and CITO setups
sections.summary: Implementation details for a 45 kg quadruped robot are presented. Pinocchio handles rigid-body kinematics and dynamics derivatives, while BPTT policy learning is performed over a short 20-control-step (0.5 s) window in a single environment.
sections.details:
Implementation specifications for simulation and physical hardware:

### VI-A Rigid-Body Dynamics and Transition Jacobian Assembly
When constructing discrete-time transition Jacobians $f_x$ and $f_u$, contact sensitivities $\partial\bm{\lambda}/\partial\bm{x}_t$ and $\partial\bm{\lambda}/\partial\bm{u}_t$ are supplied by the proposed method. Remaining rigid-body derivatives (such as contact Jacobian variations and the kinematic Hessian $\partial J_c/\partial\bm{q}$) are computed analytically using the Pinocchio library.

### VI-B Robot Model and Cost Formulation
The system is a 45 kg floating-base quadruped robot (37 state dimensions, 12 joint torque inputs). The control loop runs at 25 ms (40 Hz), with feet modeled as point contacts with Coulomb friction. Both CITO and policy learning use tracking costs penalizing errors in floating-base pose and joint angles relative to nominal targets. No contact sequences (gait schedules) are pre-specified, except for reference foot clearance in gait-conditioned tasks.

### VI-C BPTT Policy Learning Setup
RaiSim runs with a 1 ms step size, advancing 25 substeps per control step. The BPTT horizon is set to a short window of $H=20$ control steps (0.5 s). The policy is a two-layer MLP [256, 128] mapping 60-dimensional observations (velocity commands, gravity vector, joint positions/velocities, base twist, previous action) to joint PD targets. Training runs on a desktop PC (Intel Core i9-10900K CPU).

### VI-D Contact-Implicit Trajectory Optimization (CITO) Setup
For base pose reaching tasks, a Box-FDDP solver optimizes over a 20-step (0.5 s) horizon, executed sequentially in a model predictive control (MPC) receding-horizon framework.

sections.heading: Policy learning experiments: Real robot walking after under two minutes in a single environment!
sections.summary: Single-environment BPTT policy learning demonstrates that only the proposed gradient successfully acquires unconditioned gaits. A trotting policy learned in 100,000 samples and 108 seconds transferred directly (zero-shot) to physical hardware, robustly traversing debris, resisting pushes, and walking over slippery floors without falling.
sections.details:
BPTT policy learning driven by the proposed gradient achieves remarkable performance:

### VII-A Comparison Across Contact Gradients
Evaluations covered four tasks: unconditioned walking (nominal and low friction) and gait-conditioned walking (trot and pace). In unconditioned tasks, only the proposed gradient succeeded. With exact or Signorini-relaxed gradients, grounded feet remained clamped, preventing forward motion and causing the robot to pitch over. Even on low-friction ground, forward sliding alone was insufficient; gradients actively encouraging mode transitions in the backward pass were vital.

### VII-B Direct Hardware Transfer and Robustness
Policies trained with BPTT in a single environment without parallel workers were deployed directly onto a 45 kg quadruped robot without fine-tuning. Trotting and pacing policies finished training in 100,000 samples and 108 seconds, while low-friction unconditioned walking completed in 160,000 samples and 172 seconds. On hardware, the robot traversed scattered debris and recovered from lateral tugs by dynamically stepping. On floors treated with boric acid powder to create low friction ($\mu \approx 0.25$), the robot tolerated significant foot slip while correcting its posture and sustaining locomotion.

### VII-C Comparison with Model-Free Reinforcement Learning (PPO)
PPO required at least 128 parallel environments (around $10^7$ samples and 17.7 minutes) to discover a trotting gait. The proposed BPTT method matched or exceeded this tracking performance using a single environment (around $10^5$ samples and 1.8 minutes). This represents a roughly 100x reduction in sample count and a 9.8x speedup in wall-clock time.

### VII-D Numerical Behavior of the Newton Solver
Combining residual regularization $\beta$ and normal velocity offset $\delta$ allowed 99.95% of iterations to meet tolerance within 8 steps. Spurious convergence to unphysical solutions (such as interpenetration or friction-cone violations) was suppressed to just 0.0058%.

captions.F9: Training efficiency comparison between BPTT and PPO on the trotting task. (a) Proposed BPTT achieves rapid reward improvement across all environment counts from 1 to 64. (b) PPO stalls with 16 to 64 environments and only learns trotting at 128+ environments. (c) Reward vs. sample count shows BPTT (1 env) reaches competitive rewards using two orders of magnitude less data than PPO (128 envs).
captions.F7: Hardware validation of policies trained with single-environment BPTT. Snapshots and estimated contact patterns for (a) trotting, (b) pacing, and (c) unconditioned walking. Trotting and pacing took only 108 s of training, while unconditioned walking took 172 s, all transferring successfully to hardware with zero fine-tuning.
captions.F8: Hardware robustness benchmarks. (a) Traversing scattered debris. (b) Recovery response against impulsive lateral tugs while walking (velocity errors converged in all 14 trials). (c) Slip recovery on a low-friction surface coated with boric acid. Despite large roll and pitch excursions during sliding intervals, the robot sustained locomotion without falling.

sections.heading: Trajectory optimization experiments: Autonomous foot stepping and disturbance recovery
sections.summary: In contact-implicit trajectory optimization (CITO), the proposed gradient achieves the lowest tracking costs across base pose reaching benchmarks. Access to first-order tangential sensitivity enables autonomous foot repositioning and controlled sliding braking under large pull disturbances.
sections.details:
CITO experiments highlight the practical utility of the proposed gradient:

### VIII-A Contact-Implicit Base Pose Reaching Tasks
Three reaching tasks—translation, yaw rotation, and pitch rotation—were evaluated without pre-specified contact sequences. With exact gradients, feet remained stuck at their initial positions, forcing the torso to tilt or twist awkwardly and driving costs up rapidly as target displacements grew. Signorini-relaxed gradients permitted liftoff, but lacking tangential sensitivities, the optimizer could not guide feet to new positions. The proposed gradient provided coupled normal-tangential information, producing smooth stepping motions and consistently achieving the lowest tracking cost and pose error.

### VIII-B Convergence Analysis in DDP
Starting from a shared initial trajectory translating to the right, 25 DDP iterations with the proposed gradient dropped the cost from 116 to 39. During optimization, the heavily loaded rear-right leg transitioned from clamping into sliding, shifted laterally by 0.4 m, and executed a liftoff-and-touchdown cycle that leveled the base. Under baseline gradients, feet stayed clamped and costs plateaued between 95 and 98.

### VIII-C Contact-Implicit MPC Under Pull Disturbances
Periodic wire pull disturbances were applied in simulation. The robot withstood average peak pull forces of 81 N under exact gradients and 107 N under Signorini relaxation, whereas the proposed gradient sustained an average of 272 N (peaking at 350 N)—a 2.5x to 3.4x improvement. Under strong forward pulls, the robot deliberately slid its front feet to absorb momentum through friction while expanding its support polygon forward.

captions.F12: Cost comparison for base pose reaching tasks via CITO across (a) translation displacement (0.2 to 1.6 m), (b) yaw rotation (up to $\pi$ rad), and (c) pitch rotation (0.4 to 1.2 rad). Compared to exact (No Relaxation) and Signorini-relaxed gradients, the proposed method relaxing all modes and directions coupled together consistently yields the lowest cost and variance.

sections.heading: Summary and future directions
sections.summary: This work establishes an analytic contact gradient that relaxes Coulomb friction complementarity along a central path exclusively in the backward pass while maintaining physical fidelity in the forward pass. Future work points toward surface contacts, irregular terrain, and incorporating value functions for longer learning horizons.
sections.details:
This work addresses the long-standing challenge of differentiating through contact-mode switches in legged locomotion by introducing an asymmetric, backward-only analytic approach combining the de Saxcé correction with central-path relaxation. Achieving zero-shot physical robot deployment within minutes of single-environment training and generating autonomous foot stepping in trajectory optimization represent significant advancements.

Key avenues for future work include expanding beyond point-contact models to planar foot-ground interactions, uneven terrain, and generic geometries, which will require differentiating collision detection. Furthermore, while a 0.5 s BPTT horizon proved sufficient here, combining the gradient with learned value functions (critics), as in SHAC, offers a promising direction for longer-horizon tasks.

takeaways: Decoupling the architecture—retaining exact hard contact in the forward pass while relaxing the full friction cone along a central path only in the backward pass—serves as a best practice to avoid unphysical rollouts while supplying informative search gradients.
Relaxing tangential friction coupled with the normal direction, rather than normal relaxation alone, plays a decisive role in discovering contact-mode switches like stepping and sliding braking.

Given high-quality first-order gradient information, control policies that transfer zero-shot to real hardware can be trained via BPTT in a single environment within minutes, without massive parallel simulation.
limitations: The current implementation is restricted to point contacts on flat ground and does not incorporate derivatives of collision detection for surface feet or irregular terrain.
The BPTT horizon is short at 0.5 s (20 steps), meaning tasks requiring long-term horizons or highly complex sequential decisions may necessitate learned value functions.

The Newton solver for the relaxed solution can very rarely (0.0058%) converge spuriously to unphysical states (e.g., penetration), requiring an exception check that zeroes out the gradient to prevent bad parameter updates.
